plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a single right triangle drawn in plain black outline with no axes, grid, or shading. The triangle sits on a horizontal base labeled a beneath its midpoint. From the right end of that base a vertical side rises, labeled p on its outer edge. The hypotenuse slants down from the top of the vertical side to the left vertex, labeled h above its middle. A small open square at the lower right vertex marks the right angle between the base and the vertical side, and a single arc at the left vertex marks the acute angle, labeled with the Greek letter theta. The labeling is organized around theta rather than around the page: a is adjacent to theta, p is opposite it, and h is the hypotenuse, so each name states a role rather than a direction. Carrying no numbers at all, the drawing serves as the reference diagram for recovering an unknown acute angle from two known side lengths, the given pair determining which inverse trigonometric relation applies.

interactionPlan.concept: The acute angle of a right triangle can be found from any two known side lengths by identifying their roles relative to the angle and applying the corresponding inverse trigonometric function.
elements: horizontal base side
vertical right side
hypotenuse side
label 'a' (adjacent) centered below the base
label 'p' (opposite) centered to the right of the vertical side
label 'h' (hypotenuse) centered above and left of the hypotenuse
arc indicating the acute angle at the left vertex
label 'θ' inside the acute angle arc
square right-angle symbol at the bottom right vertex
dynamic formula text showing the inverse trig equation when a ratio is selected

interactions.label: Angle θ (°)
interactions.teaches: Changing the angle reshapes the triangle and alters the ratio between sides, visually demonstrating how the side proportions depend strictly on θ.
Clicking a side highlights it along with angle θ to reinforce that 'adjacent', 'opposite', and 'hypotenuse' are roles defined entirely by their position relative to θ.

interactions.label: Known sides
interactions.teaches: Selecting a pair of known sides highlights them and shows the corresponding inverse trigonometric function needed to solve for θ.

demo_steps.title: Side roles
demo_steps.narration: The sides are named by their position relative to angle θ: 'a' is adjacent to it, 'p' is opposite to it, and 'h' is the hypotenuse.

demo_steps.title: Changing the angle
demo_steps.narration: Dragging the angle slider reshapes the triangle, changing the lengths of 'p' and 'h' relative to 'a', but their structural roles relative to θ remain identical.

demo_steps.title: Inverse sine
demo_steps.narration: If we know the opposite side (p) and the hypotenuse (h), we use the inverse sine function to find θ: θ = arcsin(p/h).

demo_steps.title: Inverse tangent
demo_steps.narration: If we know the opposite (p) and adjacent (a) sides instead, we use the inverse tangent function: θ = arctan(p/a).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The position of angle θ defines which side is opposite and which is adjacent, and that specific pairing dictates whether to use arcsin, arccos, or arctan to find the unknown angle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a plain right triangle with a horizontal base and vertical right side. No axes or background grid. Use black outlines for the triangle. Place italicized labels 'a', 'p', and 'h' near the midpoints of the base, vertical side, and hypotenuse respectively. Draw an arc for angle θ at the left vertex and a right-angle square at the bottom right. The triangle must reshape dynamically when the angle slider is adjusted, keeping the right angle fixed at the bottom right. When a ratio is toggled, highlight the relevant two sides and display the corresponding inverse trig formula near the triangle.

authoredContext:
Given two sides of a right triangle like the one shown in the figure, find an angle.

An illustration of a right triangle with an angle theta. Adjacent to theta is the side a, opposite theta is the side p, and the hypoteneuse is side h.
